whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Technical Architect Evaluation exam for?

personas.label: CTA candidates preparing to apply
personas.description: You hold both architect credentials and need to clear this stage before the review board opens.

personas.label: Senior architects testing readiness
personas.description: You want an honest signal on whether your design and defence skills are board standard.

personas.label: Practice leads coaching candidates
personas.description: You prepare others for CTA and need to know what this stage actually assesses.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Technical Architect Evaluation Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: This is stage one of the CTA assessment, not a standard exam. You work through a scenario with a Salesforce evaluator, produce a design and discuss it. Its job is to confirm you are ready for the review board before you commit to the larger fee.
bullets: Not a multiple-choice exam. You are assessed on a scenario-based design and how you explain it.
Prerequisites first. Application Architect and System Architect must both be active.
It gates the board. Passing this stage is what gives you access to the review board.
Fee: third-party sources put this stage at around US$1,500, with the board separate. Confirm current fees with Salesforce.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: You are ready when you can read a scenario, produce a defensible design inside the time given, and explain each choice without notes. If you have never been challenged on a design out loud, practise that before booking.

examFormat.heading: Technical Architect Evaluation Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: This stage is a scenario-based assessment with an evaluator, not a question paper. Here is what to expect:
bestWayToPass: Read the scenario twice before designing: Most lost marks come from solving a slightly different problem from the one described.
Work to a structure: Cover data, security, integration, development lifecycle and licensing every time, so nothing is forgotten under time pressure.
Say what you rejected: Naming the alternative and why you did not take it is what demonstrates judgement.
Practise with a timer: The constraint is time, not knowledge. Produce complete designs under the clock before you book.

practiceQuestionsIntroSuffix: — practice scenario-style thinking and technical architecture concepts for the Architect Evaluation.

certificationCard.description: Stage one of the CTA assessment. You work through an enterprise scenario with a Salesforce evaluator, design a solution and discuss it. Passing opens access to the review board.

keyConcepts.h2: CTA Evaluation: Key Concepts for Success

blocks.heading: What This Stage Is For
blocks.body: The architect evaluation exists so that neither you nor Salesforce spends the time and cost of a full review board before you are ready. It uses the same raw material as the board, a hypothetical company with goals, systems and constraints, but on a smaller scale and with a single evaluator rather than a panel. Passing it is the gate to booking the board. Treat it as a genuine attempt: the skills it checks, reading requirements accurately and justifying design choices, are the same ones the board will test more harshly.

blocks.heading: Reading the Scenario Properly
blocks.body: Scenarios are written with detail that matters and detail that does not. Pull out the actual requirements, the constraints such as data residency, existing systems or budget, and the things that are merely background. The most common failure in this format is designing for the problem you expected rather than the one in front of you. Write the requirements down as a list and tick them off against your design before you present it, so you can show coverage rather than hope for it.

blocks.heading: Producing a Defensible Design
blocks.body: A good answer is complete, not clever. Cover the data model, how records are secured and shared, how systems integrate, how changes are released, and what licences the solution implies. Prefer standard platform capability over custom build, and be explicit when you are choosing custom and why. Keep the design proportionate: an enterprise scenario does not require every Salesforce product, and adding components you cannot justify creates questions you will have to answer.

blocks.heading: Explaining and Defending Choices
blocks.body: The discussion matters as much as the diagram. For each significant decision, be able to state the requirement it serves, the alternative you considered, and the trade-off you accepted. Acknowledge weaknesses before they are pointed out, which reads as analysis rather than defensiveness. If the evaluator challenges a choice, do not abandon it immediately, but do not dig in against a good argument either. Reasoned adjustment is a positive signal; capitulation and stubbornness are both negative ones.

blocks.heading: Preparing for This Stage
blocks.body: Work from full scenarios rather than topic revision. Set a timer, produce a complete design, then present it to someone who will ask why. Build a repeatable running order so coverage is automatic. Record yourself and listen for the places where you talk around a decision rather than making one. Candidates who clear this stage comfortably have usually rehearsed the full cycle, reading, designing and defending, several times before booking.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Technical Architect Evaluation Exam
scenarioTips.intro: This stage rewards accuracy and structure more than ambition. Solve exactly the problem described, and show your reasoning as you go.

blocks.heading: Requirement Coverage
blocks.body: List the stated requirements and map each to part of your design. Missing one is the most common and most avoidable failure.

blocks.heading: Handling Ambiguity
blocks.body: If something is unclear, state the assumption you are making and carry on. An explicit assumption is acceptable; a silent one is not.

blocks.heading: Clear Diagrams
blocks.body: A readable diagram you can talk through beats a dense one you cannot. Label the integrations and the data flows.

blocks.heading: Justification Framework
blocks.body: Requirement, decision, alternative considered, trade-off accepted. Apply it to every significant choice.

blocks.heading: Timed Practice
blocks.body: Knowledge is rarely the limit. Practise producing a complete design inside the time allowed.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the main purpose of the architect evaluation stage?
options: To replace the System Architect credential entirely for candidates
To award the CTA credential
To confirm a candidate is ready before they book the full review board
To test Apex coding under time pressure
sampleQuestions.explanation: It is a readiness assessment that gates access to the board, so neither side commits to the larger stage too early.
whyWrong: It does not replace any prerequisite credential.
The credential is awarded after the board, not here.
There is no coding component.

sampleQuestions.question: A scenario states that customer data must remain in the EU. A candidate's design stores it in a US-hosted system without comment. What is the problem?
options: It affects cost but not the assessment
A stated constraint has been ignored
It only matters if the evaluator asks about it
Nothing, as data location is an infrastructure concern
sampleQuestions.explanation: Constraints in the scenario are requirements. Ignoring one, especially a regulatory one, is a serious failure.
whyWrong: It is a compliance failure, not a cost question.
The candidate is expected to address it unprompted.
Data residency is an architecture decision, not someone else's problem.

sampleQuestions.question: Partway through, a candidate realises a requirement is ambiguous. What is the best approach?
options: Stop and wait for clarification
State the assumption being made and design on that basis
Ignore the requirement entirely
Design separately for every possible interpretation of the requirement
sampleQuestions.explanation: Making an assumption explicit shows judgement and lets the evaluator follow the reasoning.
whyWrong: Candidates are expected to proceed, not stall.
Ignoring a requirement loses coverage.
Designing for every interpretation produces a bloated, unfocused solution.

sampleQuestions.question: Which approach to a design decision demonstrates the judgement being assessed?
options: Deferring every decision to the client's preference
Choosing the most technically advanced option available
Using as many Salesforce products as possible
Naming the requirement, the option chosen
sampleQuestions.explanation: The assessment is about reasoning: what you chose, against what, and at what cost.
whyWrong: An unexplained client preference is not architecture.
Advanced is not the same as appropriate.
Unjustified components invite questions you cannot answer.

sampleQuestions.question: A candidate designs a custom solution for something a standard Salesforce feature already does. How is this likely to be viewed?
options: Neutrally, since both work
Positively, as it shows technical depth
Negatively, unless the candidate can justify why the standard feature was unsuitable
Positively, because custom code is a good deal more flexible in practice than configuration
sampleQuestions.explanation: Standard capability is preferred. Custom build needs a reason, such as a requirement the standard feature genuinely cannot meet.
whyWrong: They are not equivalent: custom build carries maintenance cost.
Depth is shown by judgement, not by building more.
Flexibility does not outweigh the cost without a reason.

sampleQuestions.question: What must be in place before taking this stage?
options: A completed Trailhead superbadge
Active Application Architect and System Architect credentials
Three full years of continuous Salesforce employment in an architect role
Only the Administrator credential
sampleQuestions.explanation: Both role-based architect credentials are prerequisites for the CTA path.
whyWrong: Superbadges are not a CTA prerequisite.
There is no employment-length rule.
Administrator alone is far short of the requirement.

sampleQuestions.question: Why is timed practice more useful than further reading for this stage?
options: The constraint is producing a complete design in the time given, not knowledge
Reading is discouraged by Salesforce
The scenario and its requirements are published to candidates well in advance
Timed practice guarantees a pass
sampleQuestions.explanation: Candidates at this level usually know the platform. What they lack is speed and structure under pressure.
whyWrong: Reading is useful, just not the binding constraint.
The scenario is not published beforehand.
Nothing guarantees a pass.

sampleQuestions.question: An evaluator challenges a candidate's integration choice with a reasonable objection. What is the best response?
options: Engage with the objection and adjust if the argument is sound
Change the stated requirement so that it fits the design already produced
Abandon the choice immediately
Refuse to discuss it further
sampleQuestions.explanation: Reasoned adjustment shows judgement. Both instant capitulation and stubbornness read badly.
whyWrong: The requirements are fixed.
Dropping a decision at the first challenge suggests it was never reasoned.
Refusing to engage fails the communication element.

sampleQuestions.question: Which set of areas should a complete design cover?
options: Only the integration diagram and the systems that appear on it
Only the user interface
Only the data model
Data, security and sharing, integration, development lifecycle and licensing
sampleQuestions.explanation: A complete answer addresses all of these, which is why a repeatable structure helps under time pressure.
whyWrong: Integration is one area among several.
User interface is a small part of an enterprise design.
A data model alone leaves most of the scenario unanswered.

sampleQuestions.question: How does this stage relate to the review board?
options: It is an alternative route to the credential that skips the board entirely
It is taken after the review board
They are the same assessment under two names
Passing it gives access to book the review board
sampleQuestions.explanation: The evaluation comes first and gates the board, which is the final stage.
whyWrong: There is no route to CTA that skips the board.
The order is evaluation first, then board.
They are separate stages with separate fees.

sampleQuestions.question: A candidate produces an excellent design but cannot finish explaining it in the time available. What does this suggest?
options: They need a repeatable presentation structure and timed rehearsal
Design quality on its own will be enough to carry the final result
The scenario was unfair
They should add more detail next time
sampleQuestions.explanation: Covering the required ground in the time given is part of the skill, and a set running order is how candidates achieve it.
whyWrong: An unexplained design cannot be assessed.
Time pressure is a deliberate part of the format.
More detail makes the time problem worse.

sampleQuestions.question: What should a candidate do with the stated requirements before presenting?
options: Check each one against the design and be ready to show where it is met
Prioritise only the technical ones
Summarise them back verbatim
Assume the evaluator already remembers every requirement in the scenario
sampleQuestions.explanation: Demonstrating coverage requirement by requirement is the most direct way to show the design answers the scenario.
whyWrong: Business requirements matter as much as technical ones.
Repeating them without mapping shows nothing.
The candidate must show coverage, not assume it.

sampleQuestions.question: Which is the best description of the material used in this stage?
options: A live Salesforce org to configure
A hypothetical company with goals
The candidate's own employer
A bank of multiple-choice questions
sampleQuestions.explanation: Both CTA stages are built on hypothetical enterprise scenarios.
whyWrong: There is no hands-on configuration.
Your own projects are not the basis of the assessment.
There are no multiple-choice questions.

sampleQuestions.question: A design includes middleware that the scenario does not obviously need. What is the risk?
options: It automatically fails the attempt
It shortens the discussion
The candidate must justify it, and cannot
None, as middleware is always good practice
sampleQuestions.explanation: Every component invites a question. Anything you cannot justify weakens the overall defence.
whyWrong: One unjustified component is not an automatic failure, but it does damage.
It lengthens the discussion, in the wrong way.
Middleware is a choice with costs, not a default.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the most useful form of rehearsal before this stage?
options: Reviewing other people's architecture diagrams quietly on your own
Re-reading the architect exam guides
Producing timed designs and presenting them to someone who challenges you
Memorising Salesforce limits
sampleQuestions.explanation: The format tests designing and defending under time pressure, which only live practice develops.
whyWrong: Passive review does not build the defence skill.
Those guides cover the prerequisite exams.
Limits are assumed knowledge at this level.
